paragraphs: The houndskull gets its name honestly: the visor comes to a snout, and from the side the helmet looks like a dog's skull. That shape was not decoration but deflection, and it produced one of the most recognisable silhouettes in European armour. This model keeps the hinged visor, the breath holes clustered on the right side and the mail attachment holes around the lower edge.

The mesh is 42,956 polygons and 43,266 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 11 texture maps at 4096x4096. That texture budget is where the hammer marks, the rivet heads and the polished-then-scratched steel come from, and it is what separates armour from a grey shell.
At $29 it suits historical and museum visualisation, medieval film and television, games, education material and print. On sale since 2017, kept to real-world scale so it fits a human head correctly.

Airless pump bottles are the standard for serums and creams because they keep air off the product, and their construction shows it: a transparent outer wall, an inner piston that rises as the bottle empties, a collar and a pump head with a lock ring. This set gives four of them, which is what a product line looks like on a shelf and what a mockup actually needs.

The mesh is 34,888 polygons and 34,840 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout. The transparency work is where the modelling matters: an airless bottle has a wall, a piston and a fill level, and all three have to be present for a refraction shader to produce anything convincing.

At $29 and built to StemCell specification, it is aimed at cosmetics and skincare packaging visualisation, brand mockups, e-commerce and retail renders, advertising and label design presentation. On sale since 2026.

A pediment is the triangle over a classical portico, and its whole purpose is to be looked at from below. That means the cornice mouldings, the dentils, the sculpted tympanum and the acroteria at the corners all have to be real geometry, because a texture that reads well head-on falls apart the moment the camera drops to street level and starts looking up.

The mesh is 157,636 polygons and 159,074 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps - 6 at 4096x4096 and one at 2048x2048. That combination gives crisp moulding profiles with weathered stone on top of them.
At $29 it suits architectural visualisation, classical and heritage building work, museum and civic renders, film and television, and games. On sale since 2016.

A drop-leg holster hangs from a belt loop on two straps and rides on the thigh, which is why it looks nothing like a hip holster. The platform sits flat against the leg, the holster body is angled forward for the draw, and the retention hood and the straps with their quick-release buckles are what a viewer actually notices in close-up.
The model is static, which is right for what it is: a holster does not need a rig, it needs to sit convincingly on a leg. It attaches to a figure without simulation and holds its shape.

At $29 it suits military and law enforcement visualisation, character set dressing for film, television and games, tactical equipment presentation and training material. On sale since 2015 and kept to real-world scale, so it fits a standard human figure and takes a pistol at the correct depth.

A keg is a deceptively specific object. The chime rings at top and bottom, the recessed well around the spear fitting, the stamped capacity markings and the rolled body seams are all standard, and getting the proportion between them wrong makes a keg look like a barrel with a valve. This model keeps the chimes and the well, with a logo applied to the body.

The mesh is light at 6,041 polygons and 6,111 vertices with non-overlapping UVs. That weight is deliberate: kegs appear in stacks, in cellars and behind bars, rarely one at a time, so the model has to be cheap to repeat.
At $24 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits brewery and beverage visualisation, bar and restaurant interiors, packaging and branding mockups, advertising and games. On sale since 2025.

A wall-mounted flag hangs differently from one on a mast. The pole comes out at an angle, the fabric falls into a soft diagonal drape rather than streaming, and the folds gather along the hoist edge. Getting that hang right is the whole job, because a flat flag on an angled pole immediately reads as a decal.

The mesh is 10,628 polygons and 10,631 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry spent on the drape and the finial rather than on the pole. Light enough to repeat along a facade or a street.

At $18 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits architectural exteriors, civic and government building renders, film and television set dressing, urban visualisation and games. On sale since 2024.

Crab tongs are a small tool with an unusual joint: the jaws are shaped to grip and crack a shell rather than to pick something up, and the pivot sits close to the head so the leverage lands where the shell breaks. The serrated inner faces and the sculpted finger grips are what make the tool identifiable, and both are built here as geometry.
It is modelled in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, so a brushed steel finish or a plated look goes on cleanly without fighting a mirrored layout.

At $12 this is one of the least expensive things in the catalogue, and it is priced as a prop should be: seafood restaurant and menu visualisation, food photography set dressing, kitchenware retail renders, advertising and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2025.

The iron pickaxe is the workhorse of the set - not the first tool a player makes and not the last, but the one they use for the longest stretch. Modelled as real boxes rather than a sprite, it casts proper shadows and holds its stepped silhouette from any angle, which a flat billboard cannot do.

It is 4,240 polygons and 4,242 vertices, quads only, with non-overlapping UVs and two 256x256 maps. Keeping the maps small is the point rather than a shortcut: the blocky look depends on pixels staying visibly square, and a large texture would smooth away the very thing that makes it recognisable.
At $9 it is aimed at fan animation, thumbnails, streaming overlays, game menu props, merchandise mockups and printing. On sale since 2016.

Yamal is the icebreaker with the shark's teeth painted on the bow, and that paint job is only the most obvious thing about her. The hull is shaped to ride up onto ice and break it with weight rather than cut through it, which gives the bow its distinctive rake and the hull its enormous beam. The model carries the helicopter deck, the mast array, the bollards and the reinforced bow plating.

It runs 630,166 polygons and 654,508 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 26 texture maps - 8 at 8192x8192, 11 at 4096x4096, 4 at 2048x2048 and 3 at 1024x1024. Eight maps at the largest size is what the hull needs: ice scarring, rust and repainted plates run the length of the ship.
A second build sits on this page at the same $299. Aimed at maritime and Arctic visualisation, documentary and news work, museum material, games and print. On sale since 2017.

The Citation X was for years the fastest civil aircraft in the sky short of Concorde, and it looks it: a sharply swept wing, engines set well back on the rear fuselage and a long pointed nose. This build includes the cabin, which is where a business jet is actually sold - the club seating, the tables, the sidewall panels and the galley are all modelled rather than implied behind tinted windows.

The mesh is 179,333 polygons and 191,276 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. Economical for an aircraft with a full interior, which is what lets the same asset serve an exterior ramp shot and a cabin render.

Three rigged builds share this page at the same $299, including versions prepared for Maya and for Cinema 4D. Aimed at business aviation marketing, charter and brokerage presentation, luxury travel advertising, film and television and games.

An oil field is not one machine, it is a yard full of them: pump jacks, separators, storage tanks, wellheads, flare stacks and the pipework tying them together. Any single item renders as an isolated curiosity; the collection is what lets you build a facility that looks like it produces something.

Buying the equipment as a set rather than piece by piece also keeps the scale and the surface treatment consistent across the yard, which is the detail that usually gives away a scene assembled from separate sources.

Four more collections sit on this page, priced from $259 to $419, for projects that need a wider inventory. This set at $249 is aimed at oil and gas visualisation, energy sector marketing, engineering and safety training material, infrastructure presentation and games. On sale since 2017.

A ninja character lives or dies on the rig. The pose vocabulary is crouches, rolls, wall runs and blade draws, all of which put extreme demands on the shoulders, hips and spine - exactly the places a weak rig breaks down. This build arrives rigged and prepared for Maya, so the deformation has already been solved in the application it will be animated in.
That preparation is the whole value here. A character delivered as a static mesh means rigging time before any animation can start, and rigging a figure in loose layered clothing is not a quick job.

A build prepared for Cinema 4D sits on this page at the same $199. Both are built to CheckMate specification and aimed at games, film and television, cinematic previsualisation, martial arts and action content, and interactive media. On sale since 2020.

Ballistic gel torsos are used to show what happens inside a body without opening one, and the transparency is the entire point: the ribcage, scapula, spine and trachea sit visible inside a clear form, so a path through the torso can be traced rather than described. This build models that arrangement with a female skeletal structure.

The mesh is deliberately spare at 3,384 polygons and 3,417 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. A gel block has no surface detail to carry, and the interior structures read through refraction rather than through geometry density, so weight would be wasted here.

At $189 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits forensic and ballistic visualisation, medical and trauma training material, law enforcement and defence presentation, research communication and documentary work. On sale since 2025.

A worker holding a two-handed earth auger is a specific posture: feet apart, knees slightly bent, both hands on the handles and the weight of the machine taken through the arms. That stance is what makes the figure read as working rather than as a mannequin holding a prop, and it is why the character and the tool were built together.

The mesh runs 109,352 polygons and 110,458 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, ships with 22 texture maps - 15 at 4096x4096, 6 at 2048x2048 and one at 512x512, and arrives rigged. The rig matters here: the same figure can be posed drilling, resting or carrying without being rebuilt.

At $159 it suits construction and infrastructure visualisation, landscaping and utilities presentation, safety and training material, architectural renders that need people at work, and games. On sale since 2018.
